claim: FOXP2 is overexpressed in human prostate cancer cells and prostate tumors.
source: Here, we found that FOXP2 is overexpressed in human prostate cancer cells and prostate tumors, but its expression is absent in normal prostate epithelial cells and low in benign prostatic hyperplasia.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data from 92 primary prostatic adenocarcinoma tissues and 23 matched normal tissues (Figure 1E), expression data from GTEx and SU2C datasets (Figure 1F), immunohistochemistry on 45 primary prostate tumors and 25 BPH samples (Figure 1G), and western blot analysis (Figure 1I).

claim: FOXP2 expression is absent in normal prostate epithelial cells.
source: Here, we found that FOXP2 is overexpressed in human prostate cancer cells and prostate tumors, but its expression is absent in normal prostate epithelial cells and low in benign prostatic hyperplasia.
evidence: Supported by expression data showing FOXP2 mRNA is undetectable or low in normal or immortalized human prostate epithelial cells (HPrEC and RWPE-1) (Figure 1H and I).

claim: FOXP2 expression is low in benign prostatic hyperplasia.
source: Here, we found that FOXP2 is overexpressed in human prostate cancer cells and prostate tumors, but its expression is absent in normal prostate epithelial cells and low in benign prostatic hyperplasia.
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemical assay showing no or low nuclear staining of FOXP2 in 96% (24/25) of benign prostatic tissues (Figure 1G).

claim: FOXP2 is a FOX transcription factor family member tightly associated with vocal development.
source: FOXP2 is a FOX transcription factor family member and tightly associated with vocal development.
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature on FOXP2 function (Bowers et al., 2013; Enard et al., 2009; Fisher and Scharff, 2009).

claim: Little is known regarding the link of FOXP2 to prostate cancer.
source: To date, little is known regarding the link of FOXP2 to prostate cancer.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field, supported by the novelty of the findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: High FOXP2 expression is significantly associated with high Gleason score.
source: We observed that high FOXP2 expression and frequent amplification are significantly associated with high Gleason score.
evidence: Supported by analysis of 491 human TCGA primary prostate tumors showing primary prostate tumors with FOXP2 expression had a higher Gleason grade (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A).

claim: Frequent amplification of FOXP2 is significantly associated with high Gleason score.
source: We observed that high FOXP2 expression and frequent amplification are significantly associated with high Gleason score.
evidence: Supported by analysis showing CNAs of FOXP2 were significantly associated with high Gleason scores (Gleason score ≥ 8) (OR = 2.10; 95% CI, 1.38–3.22; p=0.001) (Figure 1—figure supplement 4E).

claim: Ectopic expression of FOXP2 induces malignant transformation of mouse NIH3T3 fibroblasts.
source: Ectopic expression of FOXP2 induces malignant transformation of mouse NIH3T3 fibroblasts and human prostate epithelial cell RWPE-1.
evidence: Supported by soft agar assays showing FOXP2 can transform NIH3T3 fibroblasts, inducing loss of contact inhibition and gain of anchorage-independent growth (Figure 1J, Figure 1—figure supplement 3C and D).

claim: Ectopic expression of FOXP2 induces malignant transformation of human prostate epithelial cell RWPE-1.
source: Ectopic expression of FOXP2 induces malignant transformation of mouse NIH3T3 fibroblasts and human prostate epithelial cell RWPE-1.
evidence: Supported by assays of focus formation and anchorage-independent growth showing overexpression of FOXP2 induced malignant transformation of RWPE-1 cells (Figure 1L and M, Figure 1—figure supplement 3H).

claim: FOXP2 knockdown suppresses the proliferation of prostate cancer cells.
source: Conversely, FOXP2 knockdown suppresses the proliferation of prostate cancer cells.
evidence: Supported by data showing shRNA-mediated FOXP2 knockdown markedly inhibited the cell growth and colony-forming ability of LNCaP and PC3 cells (Figure 1N and O).

claim: Transgenic overexpression of FOXP2 in the mouse prostate causes prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia.
source: Transgenic overexpression of FOXP2 in the mouse prostate causes prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia.
evidence: Supported by data showing 97% (34/35) of FOXP2 transgenic mice developed PIN (Figure 4A, Supplementary file 1e).

claim: Overexpression of FOXP2 aberrantly activates oncogenic MET signaling.
source: Overexpression of FOXP2 aberrantly activates oncogenic MET signaling and inhibition of MET signaling effectively reverts the FOXP2-induced oncogenic phenotype.
evidence: Supported by data showing elevated phosphorylation of MET and AKT in FOXP2-transformed cells (Figure 3A), positive correlation between FOXP2 and MET pathway members (Figure 2E), and CUT&Tag identification of FOXP2-binding sites in MET and HGF (Figure 3J and K).

claim: Inhibition of MET signaling effectively reverts the FOXP2-induced oncogenic phenotype.
source: Overexpression of FOXP2 aberrantly activates oncogenic MET signaling and inhibition of MET signaling effectively reverts the FOXP2-induced oncogenic phenotype.
evidence: Supported by data showing treatment with MET inhibitor foretinib or AKT inhibitor MK2206 resulted in significantly reduced anchorage-independent growth or foci formation in FOXP2-overexpressing cells (Figure 3H and I).

claim: CUT&Tag assay identified FOXP2-binding sites located in MET.
source: CUT&Tag assay identified FOXP2-binding sites located in MET and its associated gene HGF.
evidence: Supported by CUT&Tag data showing potential FOXP2-binding fragments located in MET in prostate cancer LNCaP cells (Figure 3J and K).

claim: CUT&Tag assay identified FOXP2-binding sites located in HGF.
source: CUT&Tag assay identified FOXP2-binding sites located in MET and its associated gene HGF.
evidence: Supported by CUT&Tag data showing potential FOXP2-binding fragments located in HGF in prostate cancer LNCaP cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D).

claim: A novel recurrent FOXP2-CPED1 fusion was identified in prostate tumors.
source: Additionally, the novel recurrent FOXP2-CPED1 fusion identified in prostate tumors results in high expression of truncated FOXP2, which exhibit a similar capacity for malignant transformation.
evidence: Supported by RNA-Seq and RT-PCR combined with Sanger sequencing identifying FOXP2-CPED1 fusion in 2 of 100 indolent prostate tumors (Figure 1A and B).

claim: FOXP2-CPED1 fusion results in high expression of truncated FOXP2.
source: Additionally, the novel recurrent FOXP2-CPED1 fusion identified in prostate tumors results in high expression of truncated FOXP2, which exhibit a similar capacity for malignant transformation.
evidence: Supported by qPCR and western blot data showing increased expression of truncated FOXP2 protein in fusion-carrying tumor (Figure 1C and D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1F and G).

claim: Truncated FOXP2 from FOXP2-CPED1 fusion exhibits a similar capacity for malignant transformation as wild-type FOXP2.
source: Additionally, the novel recurrent FOXP2-CPED1 fusion identified in prostate tumors results in high expression of truncated FOXP2, which exhibit a similar capacity for malignant transformation.
evidence: Supported by soft agar assays showing FOXP2-CPED1 was able to confer oncogenic phenotype similar to FOXP2 (Figure 1J), and xenograft studies showing tumor formation in mice (Figure 1K).

claim: FOXP2 is involved in tumorigenicity of prostate.
source: Together, our data indicate that FOXP2 is involved in tumorigenicity of prostate.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by multiple lines of evidence including transformation assays, xenograft studies, and transgenic mouse models presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Prostate cancer is the second most commonly diagnosed cancer worldwide in men, with ~1.3 million new cases and ~0.36 million deaths in 2018.
source: Prostate cancer is the second most commonly diagnosed cancer worldwide in men, with ~1.3 million new cases and ~0.36 million deaths in 2018 (Culp et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Culp et al., 2020.

claim: In China, the incidence rate of prostate cancer has increased quickly, with an annual percentage change of ~13% since 2000.
source: In China, the incidence rate of prostate cancer has increased quickly, with an annual percentage change of ~13% since 2000 (Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen et al., 2016.

claim: Overexpression of ETS family genes ERG and ETV1 is involved in prostate tumorigenesis.
source: Accumulating data from genomic characterization and functional studies have revealed some oncogenes, including the E26 transformation-specific (ETS) family genes ERG and ETV1, among others, whose overexpression is involved in prostate tumorigenesis (Baena et al., 2013; Carver et al., 2009; Tomlins et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Baena et al., 2013; Carver et al., 2009; Tomlins et al., 2005.

claim: FOXP2 mutations are the only known cause of developmental speech and language disorder in humans.
source: Mutations in FOXP2 are the only known cause of developmental speech and language disorder in humans (Spiteri et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Spiteri et al., 2007.

claim: FOXP2-CPED1 fusion was identified in 2 of 100 indolent prostate tumors.
source: In this study, we identified a new gene fusion, FOXP2-CPED1, in 2 of 100 indolent prostate tumors by performing RNA sequencing and whole-genome sequencing analyzes (Figure 1A and B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–E, and Supplementary file 1a and b).
evidence: Supported by RNA-Seq and whole-genome sequencing data (Figure 1A and B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–E).

claim: FOXP2-CPED1 fusion resulted in increased expression of a truncated FOXP2 protein that retained the complete FOXP2 functional domains.
source: We found that in the prostate tumor the fusion consequently resulted in increased expression of a truncated FOXP2 protein that retained the complete FOXP2 functional domains (Spiteri et al., 2007; Hannenhalli and Kaestner, 2009; Lai et al., 2001; Shu et al., 2001), but had an aberrant C-terminus (Figure 1C and D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1F and G).
evidence: Supported by protein structure analysis (Figure 1C) and expression data (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1F and G), with citations to literature on FOXP2 functional domains.

claim: FOXP2-CPED1 fusion led to loss of the 3′UTR of FOXP2, allowing escape from regulation by miR-27a and miR-27b.
source: Mechanistically, we conducted small RNA sequencing of the fusion-positive tumor followed by functional assays, demonstrating that FOXP2-CPED1 fusion led to loss of the 3′UTR of FOXP2, thus allowing escape from regulation by miR-27a and miR-27b and consequently resulting in aberrantly high expression of the truncated FOXP2 protein with full functional domains (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H–L).
evidence: Supported by small RNA sequencing and luciferase assays showing miR-27a and miR-27b target FOXP2 3'UTR (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H–L).

claim: The FOXP2 mRNA levels were significantly increased in prostate cancer samples with respect to normal tissues.
source: The FOXP2 mRNA levels were significantly increased in prostate cancer samples with respect to normal tissues (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data from in-house samples and analysis of SU2C and GTEx datasets (Figure 1E and F).

claim: Strong or medium staining of FOXP2 protein was observed in 53% (24/45) of primary prostate adenocarcinomas.
source: Strong or medium staining of FOXP2 protein was observed in 53% (24/45) of primary prostate adenocarcinomas.
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemical assay data (Figure 1G).

claim: No or low nuclear staining of FOXP2 was observed in 96% (24/25) of benign prostatic tissues.
source: No or low nuclear staining of FOXP2 was observed in 96% (24/25) of benign prostatic tissues.
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemical assay data (Figure 1G).

claim: There was a statistically significant difference in the FOXP2 staining intensity between prostate cancer and benign prostate tissue.
source: There was a statistically significant difference in the FOXP2 staining intensity between prostate cancer and benign prostate tissue (two-tailed p=0.001, by Fisher's exact test) (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of immunohistochemical data (Figure 1G).

claim: FOXP2 expression was markedly elevated in human prostate cancer cell lines (PC3, LNCaP, VCaP, and DU145).
source: Likewise, FOXP2 expression was markedly elevated in human prostate cancer cell lines (PC3, LNCaP, VCaP, and DU145), but was undetectable or low in normal or immortalized human prostate epithelial cells (HPrEC and RWPE-1) (Figure 1H and I).
evidence: Supported by GEO database analysis (Figure 1H) and western blot data (Figure 1I).

claim: FOXP2 was undetectable or low in normal or immortalized human prostate epithelial cells (HPrEC and RWPE-1).
source: Likewise, FOXP2 expression was markedly elevated in human prostate cancer cell lines (PC3, LNCaP, VCaP, and DU145), but was undetectable or low in normal or immortalized human prostate epithelial cells (HPrEC and RWPE-1) (Figure 1H and I).
evidence: Supported by GEO database analysis (Figure 1H) and western blot data (Figure 1I).

claim: NIH3T3 fibroblasts lack endogenous Foxp2 protein expression.
source: Therefore, in this study, to explore the biological consequence of high expression of the FOXP2 gene, we first introduced the wild-type or fusion FOXP2 cDNA into mouse NIH3T3 fibroblasts that lack endogenous Foxp2 protein expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A and B)
evidence: Supported by western blot showing undetectable endogenic Foxp2 protein in parental NIH3T3 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).

claim: FOXP2 can transform NIH3T3 fibroblasts, inducing loss of contact inhibition and gain of anchorage-independent growth.
source: We found that FOXP2 can transform NIH3T3 fibroblasts, inducing loss of contact inhibition and gain of anchorage-independent growth, which are tumorigenic properties (Figure 1J, Figure 1—figure supplement 3C and D).
evidence: Supported by colony formation assays and soft agar assays (Figure 1J, Figure 1—figure supplement 3C and D).

claim: 21 of the 42 NIH3T3 cell lines expressing the FOXP2-CPED1 fusion gained the ability for anchorage-independent growth.
source: The assays showed that 21 of the 42 NIH3T3 cell lines expressing the FOXP2-CPED1 fusion gained the ability for anchorage-independent growth, as did 10 of the 32 cell lines with FOXP2 expression, indicating that FOXP2-CPED1 and FOXP2 have comparable effects on cell transformation (p=0.23, by Fisher's exact test).
evidence: Supported by soft agar colony formation assay data (Figure 1J).

claim: 10 of the 32 NIH3T3 cell lines with FOXP2 expression gained the ability for anchorage-independent growth.
source: The assays showed that 21 of the 42 NIH3T3 cell lines expressing the FOXP2-CPED1 fusion gained the ability for anchorage-independent growth, as did 10 of the 32 cell lines with FOXP2 expression, indicating that FOXP2-CPED1 and FOXP2 have comparable effects on cell transformation (p=0.23, by Fisher's exact test).
evidence: Supported by soft agar colony formation assay data (Figure 1J).

claim: FOXP2-CPED1 and FOXP2 have comparable effects on cell transformation.
source: The assays showed that 21 of the 42 NIH3T3 cell lines expressing the FOXP2-CPED1 fusion gained the ability for anchorage-independent growth, as did 10 of the 32 cell lines with FOXP2 expression, indicating that FOXP2-CPED1 and FOXP2 have comparable effects on cell transformation (p=0.23, by Fisher's exact test).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of transformation assay data showing no significant difference (p=0.23).

claim: FOXP2-overexpressing NIH3T3 cells injected into the flanks of NOD-SCID mice formed tumors in 10/15 mice.
source: We observed that FOXP2-overexpressing NIH3T3 cells injected into the flanks of NOD-SCID mice formed tumors at a higher penetrance than did parental or empty vector control cells: in 10/15 mice compared with 0/5 mice for parental cells and 0/8 for control cells (Figure 1K, Figure 1—figure supplement 3E and F).
evidence: Supported by xenograft study data (Figure 1K, Figure 1—figure supplement 3E and F).

claim: FOXP2-CPED1-overexpressing NIH3T3 cells formed tumors in 11/15 mice.
source: In 11/15 mice, FOXP2-CPED1-overexpressing NIH3T3 cells formed tumors in mice (Figure 1K, Figure 1—figure supplement 3E and F).
evidence: Supported by xenograft study data (Figure 1K, Figure 1—figure supplement 3E and F).

claim: FOXP2 overexpression significantly increased the proliferation of RWPE-1 cells relative to that of control cells.
source: We observed that FOXP2 overexpression significantly increased the proliferation of RWPE-1 cells relative to that of control cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 3G).
evidence: Supported by Celltiter-Glo assay data (Figure 1—figure supplement 3G).

claim: Overexpression of wild-type FOXP2 or FOXP2 fusion induced malignant transformation of RWPE-1 cells.
source: Similar to NIH3T3 cells, assays of focus formation and anchorage-independent growth consistently showed that overexpression of wild-type FOXP2 or FOXP2 fusion induced malignant transformation of RWPE-1 cells (Figure 1L and M, Figure 1—figure supplement 3H).
evidence: Supported by focus formation and soft agar assays (Figure 1L and M, Figure 1—figure supplement 3H).

claim: shRNA-mediated FOXP2 knockdown markedly inhibited the cell growth and colony-forming ability of LNCaP and PC3 cells.
source: We found that shRNA-mediated FOXP2 knockdown markedly inhibited the cell growth and colony-forming ability of LNCaP and PC3 cells (Figure 1N and O).
evidence: Supported by cell growth assays and focus formation assays (Figure 1N and O).

claim: Cell growth ability was decreased by Foxp2 knockdown in mouse pancreatic cancer cells.
source: Our findings were consistent with previous data showing that the cell growth ability was decreased by Foxp2 knockdown in mouse pancreatic cancer cells (Rad et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rad et al., 2015.

claim: The expression of FOXP2 was significantly correlated with the expression of 3206 genes in 255 primary prostate tumors from TCGA.
source: We observed that the expression of FOXP2 was significantly correlated with the expression of 3206 genes (refer to FOXP2 expression-correlated genes, FECGs) (|Spearman's ρ ≥ 0.5|) (Figure 2B, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of TCGA data (Figure 2B, Supplementary file 2).

claim: 18 of the 74 FECGs enriched in the PI3K-AKT pathway are known cancer driver genes.
source: Notably, 18 of the 74 FECGs enriched in the PI3K-AKT pathway are known cancer driver genes, which include 4 core members of oncogenic MET signaling (HGF, MET, PIK3R1, and PIK3CA) (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by pathway enrichment analysis (Figure 2D).

claim: 4 core members of oncogenic MET signaling (HGF, MET, PIK3R1, and PIK3CA) are among the FECGs enriched in the PI3K-AKT pathway.
source: Notably, 18 of the 74 FECGs enriched in the PI3K-AKT pathway are known cancer driver genes, which include 4 core members of oncogenic MET signaling (HGF, MET, PIK3R1, and PIK3CA) (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by pathway enrichment analysis (Figure 2D).

claim: There is a significantly positive correlation between the expression of FOXP2 and the four individual core members of MET signaling (HGF, MET, PIK3R1, and PIK3CA) across three datasets.
source: Consistently, we observed a significantly positive correlation between the expression of FOXP2 and the four individual core members of MET signaling (HGF, MET, PIK3R1, and PIK3CA) across the three datasets (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of three datasets including in-house samples, GSE54460, and Taylor dataset (Figure 2E).

claim: HGF, MET, PIK3R1, and PIK3CA were upregulated in RWPE-1 cells overexpressing FOXP2.
source: These four putative candidates were further confirmed to be upregulated in RWPE-1 cells overexpressing FOXP2 by qPCR (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data (Figure 2F).

claim: HGF, MET, and PIK3CA were downregulated in the FOXP2 knockdown PC3 prostate cancer cells.
source: Conversely, the core members (HGF, MET, and PIK3CA) were downregulated in the FOXP2 knockdown PC3 prostate cancer cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).

claim: Overexpression of FOXP2 induced elevated phosphorylation of tyrosines Y1234/1235 in the MET kinase domain in FOXP2-transformed RWPE-1 and NIH3T3 cells.
source: We observed obviously elevated phosphorylation of tyrosines Y1234/1235 in the MET kinase domain in the FOXP2-transformed RWPE-1 and FOXP2-transformed NIH3T3 cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data (Figure 3A).

claim: Overexpression of FOXP2 induced strong activation of PI3K signaling, as indicated by the elevated phosphorylation level of AKT at serine 473.
source: Furthermore, overexpression of FOXP2 induced strong activation of PI3K signaing, as indicated by the elevated phosphorylation level of AKT at serine 473 (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data (Figure 3A).

claim: AKT is a key downstream effector of HGF/MET/PI3K signaling.
source: AKT is a key downstream effector of HGF/MET/PI3K signaling (Comoglio et al., 2018) and is able to initiate prostate neoplasia in mice (Majumder et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Comoglio et al., 2018 and Majumder et al., 2003.

claim: AKT is able to initiate prostate neoplasia in mice.
source: AKT is a key downstream effector of HGF/MET/PI3K signaling (Comoglio et al., 2018) and is able to initiate prostate neoplasia in mice (Majumder et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Majumder et al., 2003.

claim: FOXP2 silencing using shRNA caused decreases in phospho-MET and phospho-AKT levels in PC3 and LNCaP prostate cancer cell lines.
source: Conversely, FOXP2 silencing using shRNA caused decreases in phospho-MET and phospho-AKT levels in two prostate cancer cell lines, PC3 and LNCaP (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by protein blot analysis (Figure 3B).

claim: Higher phosphorylation levels of MET and AKT were detected in primary human prostate tumors with higher compared with lower FOXP2 protein abundance.
source: Moreover, we detected higher phosphorylation levels of MET and AKT in primary human prostate tumors with higher compared with lower FOXP2 protein abundance (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by protein blot analysis of 18 human localized primary prostate tumors (Figure 3C).

claim: Treatment of FOXP2-overexpressing cells with foretinib resulted in twofold to threefold decreases in the IC50.
source: The FOXP2-overexpressing cells were subsequently treated with the MET tyrosine kinase inhibitor foretinib or AKT inhibitor MK2206, resulting in twofold to threefold (for foretinib) and threefold to twelvefold (for MK2206) decreases in the half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) in RWPE-1 cells and NIH3T3 cells with FOXP2 overexpression (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: Supported by IC50 assay data (Figure 3D and E).

claim: Treatment of FOXP2-overexpressing cells with MK2206 resulted in threefold to twelvefold decreases in the IC50.
source: The FOXP2-overexpressing cells were subsequently treated with the MET tyrosine kinase inhibitor foretinib or AKT inhibitor MK2206, resulting in twofold to threefold (for foretinib) and threefold to twelvefold (for MK2206) decreases in the half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) in RWPE-1 cells and NIH3T3 cells with FOXP2 overexpression (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: Supported by IC50 assay data (Figure 3D and E).

claim: Treatment of FOXP2-overexpressing cells with foretinib or MK2206 abrogated MET and/or AKT phosphorylation.
source: Furthermore, treatment of FOXP2-overexpressing RWPE-1 cells and FOXP2-overexpressing NIH3T3 cells with foretinib or MK2206 abrogated MET and/or AKT phosphorylation (Figure 3F and G)
evidence: Supported by western blot analysis (Figure 3F and G).

claim: Treatment of FOXP2-overexpressing cells with foretinib or MK2206 resulted in significantly reduced anchorage-independent growth or foci formation relative to nontreated cells.
source: Furthermore, treatment of FOXP2-overexpressing RWPE-1 cells and FOXP2-overexpressing NIH3T3 cells with foretinib or MK2206 abrogated MET and/or AKT phosphorylation (Figure 3F and G) and resulted in significantly reduced anchorage-independent growth or foci formation relative to those in nontreated cells (Figure 3I and H).
evidence: Supported by soft agar assays and focus formation assays (Figure 3H and I).

claim: siRNA-mediated knockdown of MET significantly reduced the growth of RWPE-1 cells overexpressing FOXP2 or FOXP2-CPED1.
source: We observed a decrease in both MET expression and phospho-AKT levels in these cells. Consistently, we found that siRNA-mediated knockdown of MET significantly reduced the growth of RWPE-1 cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by CellTiter-Glo assay data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).

claim: Restoration of MET does not reverse the change in viability of FOXP2 knockdown PC3 cells.
source: However, the restoration of MET does not reverse the change in viability of FOXP2 knockdown PC3 cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by cell proliferation assay data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).

claim: All ARR2PB-FOXP2 mice (n = 35) examined had hyperplasia in prostates by 46–65 wk of age.
source: By 46–65 wk of age, all ARR2PB-FOXP2 mice (n = 35) and ARR2PB-FOXP2-CPED1 mice (n = 32) examined had hyperplasia in prostates (Supplementary file 1e).
evidence: Supported by histological analysis data (Supplementary file 1e).

claim: All ARR2PB-FOXP2-CPED1 mice (n = 32) examined had hyperplasia in prostates by 46–65 wk of age.
source: By 46–65 wk of age, all ARR2PB-FOXP2 mice (n = 35) and ARR2PB-FOXP2-CPED1 mice (n = 32) examined had hyperplasia in prostates (Supplementary file 1e).
evidence: Supported by histological analysis data (Supplementary file 1e).

claim: 97% (34/35) of FOXP2 transgenic mice developed PIN.
source: Furthermore, 97% (34/35) of FOXP2 transgenic mice and 88% (28/32) of FOXP2-CPED1 mice developed PIN.
evidence: Supported by histological analysis data (Supplementary file 1e, Figure 4A).

claim: 88% (28/32) of FOXP2-CPED1 mice developed PIN.
source: Furthermore, 97% (34/35) of FOXP2 transgenic mice and 88% (28/32) of FOXP2-CPED1 mice developed PIN.
evidence: Supported by histological analysis data (Supplementary file 1e, Figure 4A).

claim: All littermate wild-type prostates had normal morphology, although they also had focal benign hyperplasia.
source: All littermate wild-type prostates had normal morphology, although they also had focal benign hyperplasia.
evidence: Supported by histological analysis.

claim: Most PINs were observed in the anterior and ventral prostate lobes, and they were all focal.
source: Most PINs were observed in the anterior and ventral prostate lobes, and they were all focal (Supplementary file 1e).
evidence: Supported by histological analysis data (Supplementary file 1e).

claim: Both transgenic FOXP2 and FOXP2-CPED1 fusion mice showed a five- to sixfold increase in the proliferation index of prostate epithelial cells in preneoplastic prostate glands compared with wild-type control mice.
source: In comparison with wild-type control mice, both transgenic FOXP2 and FOXP2-CPED1 fusion mice showed a five- to sixfold increase in the proliferation index of prostate epithelial cells in preneoplastic prostate glands, as shown by Ki67 staining (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by Ki67 immunohistochemistry data (Figure 4B).

claim: Increased phosphorylation levels of mouse Met and Akt in prostates of both FOXP2 and FOXP2-CPED1 fusion transgenic mice compared with those in prostates of control mice were observed.
source: Moreover, consistent with our in vitro data, increased phosphorylation levels of mouse Met and its downstream mediator Akt in prostates of both FOXP2 and FOXP2-CPED1 fusion transgenic mice compared with those in prostates of control mice were observed (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemical analysis (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1G).

claim: FOXP2 protein expression is absent or low in normal human prostate epithelial cells and benign prostatic hyperplasia.
source: Our findings revealed that FOXP2 protein expression is absent or low in normal human prostate epithelial cells and benign prostatic hyperplasia but is markedly increased in PIN, localized prostate tumors, and metastatic prostate cancer cell lines.
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry, western blot, and expression analysis data presented in Figure 1.

claim: FOXP2 protein expression is markedly increased in PIN, localized prostate tumors, and metastatic prostate cancer cell lines.
source: Our findings revealed that FOXP2 protein expression is absent or low in normal human prostate epithelial cells and benign prostatic hyperplasia but is markedly increased in PIN, localized prostate tumors, and metastatic prostate cancer cell lines.
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry, western blot, and expression analysis data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Primary prostate tumors with FOXP2 expression had a higher Gleason grade than cases without FOXP2 expression.
source: We found that primary prostate tumors with FOXP2 expression had a higher Gleason grade than cases without FOXP2 expression by analyzing the clinical data of 491 human TCGA primary prostate tumors (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: Supported by analysis of TCGA data (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A).

claim: Frequent amplification of the FOXP2 gene occurred in 15–20% of primary prostate tumors from the Broad/Cornell and TCGA datasets.
source: Next, we observed frequent amplification of the FOXP2 gene, which occurred in 15–20% of primary prostate tumors from the Broad/Cornell (Baca et al., 2013) and TCGA datasets and in 25% of metastatic tumors from the SU2C dataset (Robinson et al., 2015; Figure 1—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: Supported by copy number alteration analysis of Broad/Cornell and TCGA datasets (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B).

claim: Frequent amplification of the FOXP2 gene occurred in 25% of metastatic tumors from the SU2C dataset.
source: Next, we observed frequent amplification of the FOXP2 gene, which occurred in 15–20% of primary prostate tumors from the Broad/Cornell (Baca et al., 2013) and TCGA datasets and in 25% of metastatic tumors from the SU2C dataset (Robinson et al., 2015; Figure 1—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: Supported by copy number alteration analysis of SU2C dataset (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B).

claim: In 268 tumors with FOXP2 amplification at the DNA level, consistent FOXP2 mRNA overexpression was observed across most tumors (197/268).
source: Moreover, we conducted the analysis on tumors with both FOXP2 gene expression and amplification data available in the Catalogue Of Somatic Mutations In Cancer (COSMIC) datasets. In 268 tumors with FOXP2 amplification at the DNA level, we observed consistent FOXP2 mRNA overexpression across most tumors (197/268) (Figure 1—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: Supported by analysis of COSMIC datasets (Figure 1—figure supplement 4C).

claim: CNAs of FOXP2 were significantly associated with high Gleason scores (Gleason score ≥ 8) (OR = 2.10; 95% CI, 1.38–3.22; p=0.001).
source: CNAs of FOXP2 were significantly associated with high Gleason scores (Gleason score ≥ 8) (OR = 2.10; 95% CI, 1.38–3.22; p=0.001, by Fisher's exact test) and high-grade pathologic T stages (T ≥ 3a) (OR = 2.01; 95% CI, 1.26–3.21; p=0.003, by Fisher's exact test) (Figure 1—figure supplement 4E).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of 487 primary prostate tumors (Figure 1—figure supplement 4E).

claim: CNAs of FOXP2 were significantly associated with high-grade pathologic T stages (T ≥ 3a) (OR = 2.01; 95% CI, 1.26–3.21; p=0.003).
source: CNAs of FOXP2 were significantly associated with high Gleason scores (Gleason score ≥ 8) (OR = 2.10; 95% CI, 1.38–3.22; p=0.001, by Fisher's exact test) and high-grade pathologic T stages (T ≥ 3a) (OR = 2.01; 95% CI, 1.26–3.21; p=0.003, by Fisher's exact test) (Figure 1—figure supplement 4E).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of 487 primary prostate tumors (Figure 1—figure supplement 4E).

claim: CNAs of FOXP2 were prominently enriched in ETS fusion-negative prostate tumors from the MSKCC/DFCI dataset (p=2.42 × 10–6).
source: In addition, we found that CNAs of FOXP2 were prominently enriched in ETS fusion-negative prostate tumors from the MSKCC/DFCI dataset (n = 685) (Armenia et al., 2018) (p=2.42 × 10–6, by Fisher's exact test) (Figure 1—figure supplement 4F), suggesting that FOXP2 CNAs and ETS fusions were partially mutually exclusive.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of MSKCC/DFCI dataset (Figure 1—figure supplement 4F).

claim: FOXP2 CNAs and ETS fusions were partially mutually exclusive.
source: In addition, we found that CNAs of FOXP2 were prominently enriched in ETS fusion-negative prostate tumors from the MSKCC/DFCI dataset (n = 685) (Armenia et al., 2018) (p=2.42 × 10–6, by Fisher's exact test) (Figure 1—figure supplement 4F), suggesting that FOXP2 CNAs and ETS fusions were partially mutually exclusive.
evidence: This is inferred from the statistical enrichment of FOXP2 CNAs in ETS fusion-negative tumors.

claim: Stumm et al. reported moderate to strong FOXP2 protein expression in 75% of prostate tumors.
source: Similar to our observation, Stumm et al. reported moderate to strong FOXP2 protein expression in 75% of prostate tumors, and a higher protein expression level of FOXP2 was correlated with higher Gleason score, advanced T stage, and earlier cancer recurrence in ERG fusion-negative prostate cancers (Stumm et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Stumm et al., 2013.

claim: A higher protein expression level of FOXP2 was correlated with higher Gleason score, advanced T stage, and earlier cancer recurrence in ERG fusion-negative prostate cancers.
source: Similar to our observation, Stumm et al. reported moderate to strong FOXP2 protein expression in 75% of prostate tumors, and a higher protein expression level of FOXP2 was correlated with higher Gleason score, advanced T stage, and earlier cancer recurrence in ERG fusion-negative prostate cancers (Stumm et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Stumm et al., 2013.

claim: The truncated FOXP2 protein from FOXP2-CPED1 fusion retained the full forkhead DNA binding domain (DBD).
source: The truncated FOXP2 protein retained the full forkhead DNA binding domain (DBD).
evidence: Supported by protein structure analysis (Figure 1C).

claim: Mutations in the DBD of FOXP2 cause severe autosomal-dominant disorders of speech and language in humans.
source: In humans, mutations in the DBD of FOXP2 cause severe autosomal-dominant disorders of speech and language (Lai et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lai et al., 2001.

claim: The DBD of some FOX family proteins was crucial for the growth and invasion of tumors.
source: Several lines of evidence also showed that the DBD of some other FOX family proteins was crucial for the growth and invasion of tumors (Gormally et al., 2014; Huang et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gormally et al., 2014 and Huang et al., 2015.

claim: 60 common genes were found between significantly differentially expressed genes in FOXP2-transformed NIH3T3 cells and FOXP2 expression-correlated genes in TCGA primary prostate tumors.
source: To identify genes that are significantly regulated by FOXP2, we compared two sources of differential gene expression data from TCGA primary prostate tumors and our FOXP2-transformed NIH3T3 cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E). We found 60 common genes whose expression was significantly correlated with FOXP2 expression.
evidence: Supported by comparative analysis of gene expression data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).

claim: The overlapping genes included five known cancer driver genes (including HGF, MET, and PIK3R1).
source: The overlapping genes included five known cancer driver genes (including HGF, MET, and PIK3R1) (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and E)
evidence: Supported by gene overlap analysis (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and E).

claim: The overlapping genes included five putative FOXP2 targets, such as MET and PIK3R1, identified by chromatin immunoprecipitation assays in both mice and humans.
source: The overlapping genes included five known cancer driver genes (including HGF, MET, and PIK3R1) (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and E) and five putative FOXP2 targets (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E), such as MET and PIK3R1, identified by chromatin immunoprecipitation assays in both mice and humans (Spiteri et al., 2007; Xu et al., 2022; Mukamel et al., 2011; Vernes et al., 2011; Vernes et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to chromatin immunoprecipitation studies (Spiteri et al., 2007; Xu et al., 2022; Mukamel et al., 2011; Vernes et al., 2011; Vernes et al., 2007) and gene overlap analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).

claim: MET protein expression is absent in epithelial cells of normal prostate glands and low in benign prostate hyperplasia.
source: Immunohistochemical staining of normal and malignant human prostate samples showed that MET protein expression is absent in epithelial cells of normal prostate glands and low in benign prostate hyperplasia, whereas it is frequently detected in PIN, localized and metastatic prostate tumors (Nakashiro et al., 2003; Pisters et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations to Nakashiro et al., 2003 and Pisters et al., 1995.

claim: MET protein is frequently detected in PIN, localized and metastatic prostate tumors.
source: Immunohistochemical staining of normal and malignant human prostate samples showed that MET protein expression is absent in epithelial cells of normal prostate glands and low in benign prostate hyperplasia, whereas it is frequently detected in PIN, localized and metastatic prostate tumors (Nakashiro et al., 2003; Pisters et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations to Nakashiro et al., 2003 and Pisters et al., 1995.

claim: Transgenic overexpression of Met in mouse prostate epithelial cells is sufficient to induce PIN under HGF conditions.
source: Transgenic overexpression of Met in mouse prostate epithelial cells is sufficient to induce PIN under HGF conditions and markedly promotes prostate tumor initiation, invasion and metastasis in a Pten-deficient background (Mi et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mi et al., 2018.

claim: Transgenic overexpression of Met markedly promotes prostate tumor initiation, invasion and metastasis in a Pten-deficient background.
source: Transgenic overexpression of Met in mouse prostate epithelial cells is sufficient to induce PIN under HGF conditions and markedly promotes prostate tumor initiation, invasion and metastasis in a Pten-deficient background (Mi et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mi et al., 2018.

claim: Treatment of both PC3 and LNCaP prostate tumor cells with a MET inhibitor resulted in reduced cell proliferation.
source: In agreement with our findings, treatment of both PC3 and LNCaP prostate tumor cells with a MET inhibitor resulted in reduced cell proliferation (Tu et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tu et al., 2010.

claim: MET is a receptor tyrosine kinase that is activated by its ligand, hepatocyte growth factor (HGF).
source: MET is a receptor tyrosine kinase that is activated by its ligand, hepatocyte growth factor (HGF), and this activation triggers transphosphorylation of MET (Bardelli et al., 1999; Bottaro et al., 1991; Cooper, 1992; Hov et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bardelli et al., 1999; Bottaro et al., 1991; Cooper, 1992; Hov et al., 2004.

claim: Activation of MET by HGF triggers transphosphorylation of MET.
source: MET is a receptor tyrosine kinase that is activated by its ligand, hepatocyte growth factor (HGF), and this activation triggers transphosphorylation of MET (Bardelli et al., 1999; Bottaro et al., 1991; Cooper, 1992; Hov et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bardelli et al., 1999; Bottaro et al., 1991; Cooper, 1992; Hov et al., 2004.

claim: A positive correlation exists between the expression of both MET and HGF and the expression of FOXP2 in prostate cancer tissues, FOXP2-overexpressing RWPE-1 cells, and FOXP2-overexpressing NIH3T3 cells.
source: In our study, we found a positive correlation between the expression of both MET and HGF and the expression of FOXP2 in prostate cancer tissues, FOXP2-overexpressing human prostate epithelial cells RWPE-1, and FOXP2-overexpressing NIH3T3 cells.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data showing upregulation of HGF and MET in FOXP2-overexpressing cells (Figure 2E, F) and correlation analysis.

claim: Phase III clinical trials showed that the MET kinase inhibitor cabozantinib has some clinical activity in patients with advanced prostate cancer.
source: Phase III clinical trials have shown that the MET kinase inhibitor cabozantinib has some clinical activity in patients with advanced prostate cancer, including conferring improvements in the bone scan response, radiographic progression-free survival, and circulating tumor cell conversion, although it failed to significantly improve overall survival (Smith et al., 2016; Sonpavde et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Smith et al., 2016 and Sonpavde et al., 2020.

claim: Cabozantinib failed to significantly improve overall survival in patients with advanced prostate cancer.
source: Phase III clinical trials have shown that the MET kinase inhibitor cabozantinib has some clinical activity in patients with advanced prostate cancer, including conferring improvements in the bone scan response, radiographic progression-free survival, and circulating tumor cell conversion, although it failed to significantly improve overall survival (Smith et al., 2016; Sonpavde et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Smith et al., 2016 and Sonpavde et al., 2020.

claim: MET inhibition was only effective in prostate cancer cells with MET activation.
source: Qiao et al., 2016 provided experimental evidence that MET inhibition was only effective in prostate cancer cells with MET activation.
evidence: Supported by citation to Qiao et al., 2016.

claim: FOXP2-overexpressing cells were more sensitive to inhibitors of the MET signaling pathway than control cells.
source: We observed that FOXP2-overexpressing cells were more sensitive to inhibitors of the MET signaing pathway than control cells.
evidence: Supported by IC50 assay data showing decreased IC50 values in FOXP2-overexpressing cells treated with foretinib or MK2206 (Figure 3D and E).

claim: Aberrant FOXP2 expression activates MET signaling pathway in prostate cancer with potential therapeutic implication.
source: In summary, our data indicated that FOXP2 possesses an oncogenic potential and is involved in tumorigenicity of prostate. Aberrant FOXP2 expression activates MET signaing pathway in prostate cancer with potential therapeutic implication.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by multiple lines of evidence including correlation analysis, CUT&Tag data, and drug sensitivity assays presented throughout the manuscript.
